subject: chemistry-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Electron sharing reactions
themeLabel: What are the mechanisms of chemical change?
bigPicture: Some reactions run on single electrons. Radicals, species with an unpaired electron, form when a bond splits evenly, and they are so reactive that they set off chain reactions, such as the substitution of alkanes by halogens in UV light.

keyIdeas.answer: A species with an unpaired electron, shown with a dot: Cl•, •CH₃. Very reactive because the electron seeks to pair.

Homolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks and each atom keeps one electron. Halogen molecules split in UV light or heat: Cl₂ → 2Cl• (initiation). Show single-electron movement with fish-hook (single-barbed) arrows.

keyIdeas.cue: How do alkanes react with halogens?
keyIdeas.answer: Alkanes are unreactive because C–C and C–H bonds are strong and almost non-polar. In UV light: initiation Cl₂ → 2Cl•; propagation Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃, then •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (radical regenerated); termination: two radicals combine (Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆). Gives a mixture of products, including further substitution (CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄).

keyTerms.def: Bond breaking where each fragment gets one electron.
Step where a radical reacts and makes another radical.
Step where two radicals join, removing radicals.

workedExamples.title: Mechanism
workedExamples.prompt: Write the mechanism for ethane + bromine in UV light to form bromoethane.
steps: Propagation: Br• + C₂H₆ → HBr + •C₂H₅; •C₂H₅ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + Br•.

misconceptions.right: Propagation keeps the number of radicals the same; termination removes them.
Further substitution and termination give a mixture.

misconceptions.wrong: UV breaks C–H bonds to start the reaction.
misconceptions.right: UV splits the weaker halogen–halogen bond.

practice.prompt: Explain why alkanes are generally unreactive.
checkpoints: Bonds are essentially non-polar, so not attacked by nucleophiles/electrophiles

practice.prompt: Outline the three stages of the reaction between methane and chlorine with one equation for each.

paper1A.stem: What type of bond breaking starts the chlorination of methane?

paper1B.data: Bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹, booklet): C–H 414, Cl–Cl 242, Br–Br 193.
paper1B.prompt: Explain which bond UV light breaks in initiation.
paper1B.answer: The halogen–halogen bond: it is much weaker than C–H, so UV photons have enough energy to split Cl–Cl (or Br–Br) homolytically.
